title: TCP, UDP, QUIC and HTTP/1.1, 2, 3 for designers
scopeHtml: Scope: TCP handshake, reliability and congestion control, head-of-line blocking, UDP, QUIC, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and how to choose protocols and timeouts.

notes.title: TCP in plain words
notes.html:
TCP gives two programs a reliable, ordered stream of bytes over an unreliable network. The internet itself only moves loose packets that can be lost, duplicated or reordered. TCP numbers every byte, the receiver acknowledges what it got, and the sender resends what is missing.

Starting a connection is the three-way handshake: client sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, client sends ACK. That is 1 round trip (RTT) before the first data byte can be sent (the client can send data with its ACK). Closing uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and the side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT (commonly 60 s on Linux) so late packets do not confuse a new connection.

Client                      Server
  | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------> |
  | <--- SYN-ACK (y, x+1) -- |    1 RTT
  | ---- ACK (y+1) + data -> |

Worked example. RTT Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms. A fresh connection spends 200 ms in the handshake before sending anything. A mobile app that opens a new connection per request pays this every time; one that reuses a connection pays it once.

Industry examples. Every database driver uses a connection pool (HikariCP, pgbouncer) mostly to avoid this setup cost, plus per-connection memory on the server (Postgres uses a process per connection, about 5 to 10 MB each).

Everyday analogy. A phone call: "Hello?" "Hello, who is this?" "It's me." Only then do you start talking, and you hang up politely at the end.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the handshake RTT when computing latency.
  • Not knowing TIME_WAIT: thousands of short outbound connections can exhaust local ports (ephemeral range about 28k ports by default, net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range).
  • Saying TCP is "faster" than UDP. It is more reliable, not faster.

notes.title: TCP reliability, flow control and congestion control
notes.html:
Three separate mechanisms, often confused.

  1. Reliability: sequence numbers plus ACKs plus retransmit timers. Fast retransmit resends after 3 duplicate ACKs, without waiting for the timeout.
  2. Flow control: the receiver advertises a window (how much buffer it has left) so a fast sender does not drown a slow receiver. Protects the receiver.
  3. Congestion control: the sender limits itself by a congestion window (cwnd) to avoid overloading the network. It starts small (slow start: initial cwnd of 10 segments, about 14 KB, doubling every RTT) and then grows slowly; on packet loss it shrinks. Algorithms: Reno, CUBIC (Linux default), BBR (Google, models bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to loss).

Worked example. Fetching 1 MB over a fresh connection with RTT 100 ms: slow start sends 14 KB, then 28, 56, 112, 224, 448 KB... roughly 6 round trips to deliver 1 MB, so about 600 ms plus handshake, even on a 1 Gbps link. Bandwidth is not the limit, round trips are. This is why small pages, early connection reuse and CDNs near the user matter. Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x RTT: 100 Mbps x 100 ms = 1.25 MB must be "in flight" to fill the pipe, so windows must be large enough (window scaling).

Industry examples. Google deployed BBR on YouTube and google.com, reporting throughput gains on lossy long links. CDNs tune initial cwnd and use TCP tuning for large video chunks.

Decision gravity. Changing congestion control (sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr) is a reversible per-host setting, but behaves differently with other flows on shared links; test it.

Everyday analogy. Filling a bucket through a pipe: flow control is "the bucket says it is almost full", congestion control is "the pipe in the street is jammed, trickle slowly and speed up carefully".

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up flow control (receiver) and congestion control (network).
  • Thinking more bandwidth fixes slow downloads on high-latency links.
  • Forgetting slow start restarts after idle periods unless disabled (tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0).

notes.title: Head-of-line blocking and TCP's limits
notes.html:
TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it until it is resent. This is head-of-line (HOL) blocking at the transport layer. If you multiplex 10 requests over one TCP connection (HTTP/2) and one packet is lost, all 10 streams stall waiting for the retransmit, although only one stream owned the lost packet.

Other TCP limits for designers: the handshake RTT, slow start per connection, the connection is tied to the IP:port 4-tuple (a phone switching from Wi-Fi to 4G breaks it), and the protocol is baked into operating system kernels and middleboxes, so it is very hard to change.

Worked example. 2% packet loss on a mobile network, RTT 80 ms. Each loss costs at least 1 RTT (fast retransmit), more with timeout (200 ms or more). On HTTP/2 over TCP, loss stalls all parallel streams; on HTTP/3 only the affected stream waits. Measured gains of HTTP/3 are largest on poor networks.

Industry examples. This was the key motivation for QUIC at Google and for HTTP/3 deployment at Cloudflare, Meta and Google. Meta reported lower request errors and tail latency with QUIC in their mobile apps.

Everyday analogy. A single-lane road: one broken-down car holds up all the cars behind, even those going to different towns.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/2 removed head-of-line blocking entirely. It removed it at the HTTP layer only.
  • Not realising a connection breaks when the client IP changes.

notes.title: UDP and when to use it
notes.html:
UDP just sends a packet and does not care what happens next. No handshake, no ordering, no retransmission, no congestion control. Header is 8 bytes versus 20 or more for TCP. The application adds whatever reliability it needs.

Good for: DNS (one request, one reply), live video and voice (an old frame is useless, so do not wait for a resend), games, metrics (StatsD), service discovery, and as the base for QUIC and WebRTC. Bad for: anything where you need every byte in order unless you build it yourself.

         TCP                          UDP
 handshake, ordered, retransmit    fire and forget, 8-byte header
 one stream of bytes               independent datagrams
 congestion controlled             you must control rate yourself

Worked example. A game sending position updates 30 times per second. If packet 17 is lost, TCP would stall packets 18 to 20 until 17 is resent (about 1 RTT); UDP simply uses packet 18, a fresher update. Packet size: keep under about 1,200 to 1,400 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation (MTU 1,500 typical; QUIC uses a minimum 1,200 bytes).

Industry examples. DNS, NTP, DHCP, Zoom/Meet/WebRTC media, Statsd/Datadog agent metrics, Valve game servers, and QUIC underlying HTTP/3.

Decision gravity. Choosing UDP means you own reliability and congestion fairness: powerful but expensive in engineering. Usually you adopt QUIC or an existing protocol rather than invent one. Reversible only if clients can be updated.

Everyday analogy. Dropping postcards in a letterbox versus registered courier: postcards are cheap and fast, but some never arrive.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying UDP is "unreliable so never use it". Many critical systems use it on purpose.
  • Sending large UDP datagrams that get fragmented and silently dropped.
  • Forgetting UDP has no congestion control, so a flood can hurt others.

notes.title: QUIC
notes.html:
QUIC is a modern transport built on UDP that gives you TCP-like reliability, TLS 1.3 security and multiple independent streams in one protocol. It runs in user space (app/library), so it can evolve quickly, unlike kernel TCP. It is the transport of HTTP/3.

What it fixes:

  • Faster setup: transport and TLS handshake are combined: 1 RTT for a new connection, 0-RTT to a server you have talked to before (data sent in the first flight, with replay-attack risk, so only for idempotent requests).
  • No cross-stream HOL blocking: each stream has its own ordering; loss on one stream does not stall others.
  • Connection migration: a connection is identified by a connection ID, not the IP:port, so a phone moving from Wi-Fi to 4G keeps the same connection.
  • Always encrypted, including most headers, which also stops middleboxes from ossifying the protocol.

Costs: more CPU (user-space packet handling, encryption per packet; early reports of 2x CPU versus TCP), some networks block or throttle UDP 443 so clients must fall back to TCP, and load balancers need QUIC awareness (route by connection ID).

Worked example. RTT 100 ms. HTTP/2 over TCP + TLS 1.3 on a new connection: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 200 ms before the request. HTTP/3: 1 RTT = 100 ms. On a resumed connection with 0-RTT: 0 ms of setup, request goes out immediately.

Industry examples. Google invented it (gQUIC) and standardised it as RFC 9000 in 2021. Cloudflare, Fastly, Meta, YouTube and Cloudflare-fronted sites serve large shares of traffic over HTTP/3. Nginx and Envoy support it; many origins still use HTTP/1.1 or 2 behind the CDN.

Decision gravity. Enabling HTTP/3 at the CDN edge is cheap and reversible (clients fall back). Running QUIC end to end internally costs CPU and tooling maturity; most teams keep it at the edge only.

Everyday analogy. A shipping container that already contains separate boxes and a lock: one trip delivers several independent parcels, and if you change lorries the container keeps its tracking number.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying QUIC is "UDP so unreliable". QUIC adds its own reliability and congestion control.
  • Forgetting 0-RTT replay risk and the need for TCP fallback.
  • Ignoring that firewalls dropping UDP break it unless fallback exists.

notes.title: HTTP/1.1
notes.html:
HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, as text. Messages look like GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1, headers, blank line, body. Keep-Alive (default in 1.1) reuses the connection. Pipelining existed in theory but was broken in practice (still strict order, HOL at HTTP level), so browsers turned it off.

Because one connection handles one request at a time, browsers open about 6 parallel connections per host. Developers used workarounds: domain sharding (img1.site.com, img2.site.com), sprite sheets, file bundling. Headers (cookies, user agent) are repeated in full every request, often 500 B to several KB.

GET /api/orders/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.com
Accept: application/json
Connection: keep-alive

Worked example. A page with 60 small resources over HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections: 10 rounds of fetches. At 50 ms RTT that is about 500 ms of pure waiting even with a fast server. Hence bundling.

Industry examples. Still used for simple internal service calls, webhooks and many health checks. Stripe's and GitHub's public APIs work fine over 1.1; the connection pool size matters more than the protocol.

Everyday analogy. A shop counter with one customer at a time; to go faster you open several counters (connections).

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing keep-alive is the default and what happens when idle timeouts of server and load balancer disagree (client sends on a connection the server just closed, giving random resets; set client idle timeout lower than the LB idle timeout, e.g. AWS ALB default 60 s).
  • Confusing pipelining with multiplexing.

notes.title: HTTP/2
notes.html:
HTTP/2 sends many requests at once over one TCP connection using binary frames. Each request/response is a stream with an ID; frames from different streams are interleaved, so a slow response no longer blocks a fast one at the HTTP level.

Features:

  • Multiplexing: hundreds of concurrent streams on 1 connection (SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, commonly 100 to 128).
  • HPACK header compression: repeated headers become tiny references.
  • Binary framing, stream priorities (largely replaced), flow control per stream.
  • Server push: mostly deprecated; Chrome removed it.
  • Requires TLS in practice (browsers only do h2 over HTTPS, negotiated via ALPN).

Weakness: all streams ride one TCP connection, so TCP HOL blocking hurts (see above). Also one connection means one congestion window and, with L4 load balancers, one backend: a few heavy gRPC connections can pile on a single server, so use L7 balancing for gRPC.

Worked example. Same 60 resources, one connection, all requested at once: about 1 RTT after the handshake plus transfer time, so the 500 ms example becomes roughly 100 ms. Domain sharding now hurts (extra handshakes, lost shared compression).

Industry examples. gRPC is built on HTTP/2. Nginx, Envoy, CloudFront and ALB speak h2 to clients. Most major websites use it.

Decision gravity. Moving from 1.1 to 2 at the edge is reversible and mostly free. For internal gRPC, the choice (HTTP/2 + protobuf) shapes the whole service contract and is a one-way-ish door.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant with one waiter who takes all your orders at once and brings dishes as they are ready, instead of waiting for each plate to be finished.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming HTTP/2 solves head-of-line blocking completely.
  • Putting an L4 balancer in front of gRPC and getting lopsided load.
  • Still recommending bundling and domain sharding under h2.

notes.title: HTTP/3
notes.html:
HTTP/3 is HTTP semantics (same methods, headers, status codes) over QUIC instead of TCP. To your application code nothing changes; the difference is below.

Differences from HTTP/2: transport is QUIC/UDP, so no TCP HOL blocking; header compression is QPACK (redesigned to avoid blocking across streams); setup is 1 RTT or 0-RTT; connection survives network change.

Discovery: a client does not know a server speaks h3, so it first connects with h2 over TCP, the server answers with an Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 header (or the HTTPS DNS record), and the client upgrades next time, racing both.

Comparison.

HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3
Transport TCP TCP QUIC over UDP
Parallelism 6 connections multiplexed streams multiplexed streams
HOL blocking HTTP + TCP TCP only none across streams
Header compression none HPACK QPACK
New connection (with TLS 1.3) 2 RTT 2 RTT 1 RTT (0-RTT resume)
Survives IP change no no yes

Industry examples. Google, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and Cloudflare serve h3 widely; Nginx (1.25+), Envoy, Caddy and CloudFront support it. Gains are biggest on lossy mobile links, small on fast wired links.

Decision gravity. Turn on at the edge/CDN: low risk, reversible. Do not make business logic depend on it. Keep h2 and h1 working as fallback.

Everyday analogy. The same delivery menu (HTTP) but a better courier service (QUIC) that handles each parcel separately and follows you when you move house.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing HTTP/3 changes API semantics or needs code changes.
  • Forgetting UDP 443 must be open and fallback exists.
  • Claiming h3 is always faster; on clean networks the difference is small and CPU is higher.

notes.title: Choosing a protocol and connection settings
notes.html:
Decision guide for a designer.

  • Public web/mobile API: terminate h2/h3 at a CDN or L7 load balancer; origin can be h1.1 or h2.
  • Service to service, high volume: gRPC (h2) with client-side or L7 load balancing; or HTTP/1.1 with a keep-alive pool for simplicity.
  • Real time with bi-directional data: WebSocket (over h1.1 upgrade) or WebTransport (h3) or SSE.
  • Live media or games: UDP / WebRTC / QUIC.
  • Plain queries and metrics at massive scale: UDP fire-and-forget (StatsD), accepting loss.

Connection tuning knobs worth knowing (typical values):

# Typical settings to align (illustrative)
client_idle_timeout: 45s        # must be < server/LB idle timeout
alb_idle_timeout: 60s           # AWS ALB default
server_keepalive_timeout: 75s   # nginx keepalive_timeout is a common value
max_connections_per_host: 50    # HTTP client pool
connect_timeout: 1s
read_timeout: 3s
tcp_keepalive: 30s

Production incident pattern. Sporadic connection reset or 502 on idle clients: server/LB closed an idle connection and the client reused it. Metric: spike of 502/504 and connection reset by peer after quiet periods. Fix: client idle timeout < LB idle timeout, enable retry on idempotent requests.

Another pattern: connection storm after a deploy: every client reconnects at once, doing TCP + TLS handshakes together and saturating CPU. Fix: jitter, connection draining, gradual rollout.

Industry examples. Google uses QUIC at the edge and internal RPC (Stubby/gRPC) inside. Cloudflare terminates h3 at the edge and speaks h1/h2 to origins. Uber moved mobile traffic to QUIC for tail-latency gains.

Everyday analogy. Choose transport like a vehicle: lorry (TCP) for guaranteed freight, motorbike (UDP) for fast light deliveries where a lost one does not matter, and a modern courier (QUIC) for both.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a protocol without saying the network conditions (mobile versus data centre).
  • No timeouts at all: unbounded waits exhaust threads (always set connect and read timeouts).
  • Mismatched idle timeouts between client, LB and server.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• TCP: reliable ordered byte stream, 1 RTT handshake, flow control (receiver), congestion control (network, slow start), but head-of-line blocking and IP-tied connections.
  • UDP: no handshake, order or retransmit; right for DNS, voice, games, metrics, and as the base for QUIC.
  • QUIC: UDP-based, TLS 1.3 built in, 1-RTT/0-RTT setup, independent streams, connection migration; costs CPU and needs TCP fallback.
  • HTTP/1.1: one request per connection at a time, 6 connections per host; HTTP/2: multiplexed streams on one TCP connection, HPACK; HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC with QPACK.
  • Latency is round trips: fresh TCP+TLS1.3 = 2 RTT, QUIC = 1 RTT, resumed 0-RTT. Reuse connections.
  • Use h2/h3 at the edge, gRPC or pooled h1.1 inside; align idle timeouts (client < LB < server) and always set connect/read timeouts.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how a TCP connection starts and ends. Why does it matter for latency in a system design?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you count round trips when estimating latency and know the cost of short-lived connections.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, which costs one round trip before I can send data (data can ride on the final ACK). Closing uses FIN/ACK in each direction, and whoever closes first sits in TIME_WAIT, about 60 s on Linux. So a new connection per request pays one RTT every time, plus TLS on top, and burns ports. I reuse connections with pools and keep-alive.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
TCP numbers every byte. The handshake exchanges initial sequence numbers so both sides agree where the stream starts.

Client                      Server
  | ---- SYN (seq=x) ------> |
  | <--- SYN-ACK (y, x+1) -- |    1 RTT
  | ---- ACK (y+1) + data -> |

Mumbai to Virginia is about 200 ms RTT, so a fresh connection spends 200 ms before the first request byte. TIME_WAIT exists so that delayed packets of the old connection cannot be mistaken as part of a new one on the same 4-tuple. The side that closes first holds the state. Many short outbound connections therefore pile up TIME_WAIT sockets and can exhaust the ephemeral port range (about 28k ports by default, net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the handshake RTT (and TLS RTTs) when computing latency.
  • Saying TIME_WAIT is a bug to disable. It protects correctness.
  • Saying TCP is faster than UDP. It is more reliable, not faster.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do DB drivers use pools? -> Avoid handshake cost and per-connection server memory (Postgres is a process per connection, about 5-10 MB).
  2. Who ends up in TIME_WAIT? -> The side that closes first; so let the server close, or reuse connections.
  3. Can TIME_WAIT exhaust a server? -> Mostly the client side running out of ephemeral ports for one destination IP:port; widen the range, reuse connections, add destination IPs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE draws the three arrows. Senior converts it to milliseconds for a stated RTT, ties it to pooling, and names port exhaustion as the failure mode.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service called an internal API with a new connection per call and failed with "cannot assign requested address" under load; a keep-alive pool fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between TCP flow control and congestion control, and what limits how fast one connection can send?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These two are constantly mixed up; it shows whether you can reason about throughput on long links.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Flow control protects the receiver: it advertises a window of free buffer. Congestion control protects the network: the sender keeps a congestion window (cwnd) that starts small and grows, shrinking on loss. Sending rate is bounded by the smaller of the two windows divided by RTT. Hence on a long fat link the limit is round trips, not bandwidth.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reliability (sequence numbers, ACKs, fast retransmit after 3 duplicate ACKs) is a third separate mechanism.

  • Slow start: initial cwnd 10 segments (about 14 KB), doubling each RTT, then slower growth (CUBIC, Linux default). BBR models bandwidth and RTT instead of reacting to loss.
  • Throughput <= min(rwnd, cwnd) / RTT.
  • Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x RTT: 100 Mbps x 100 ms = 1.25 MB must be in flight to fill the pipe, which needs window scaling.
Sender --(limited by cwnd: network)--> Network --(limited by rwnd: receiver)--> Receiver

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control          # cubic by default
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0  # do not restart slow start on idle keep-alive
ss -ti dst 10.0.0.5                              # shows cwnd, rtt, rcv_space per connection

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing the two up.
  • Believing more bandwidth fixes slow downloads on high-latency links.
  • Forgetting slow start restarts after idle unless disabled.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 1 MB over a fresh connection at 100 ms RTT? -> 14, 28, 56, 112, 224, 448 KB: about 6 RTT, 600 ms plus handshake.
  2. Why do CDNs help? -> Shorter RTT per round trip and warm, tuned connections.
  3. When would you pick BBR? -> Lossy or long links where loss-based CUBIC under-uses the pipe; it is a reversible per-host sysctl but test fairness against other flows.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE defines both. Senior computes the round trips and BDP and concludes that fixing RTT (CDN, reuse) beats buying bandwidth.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cross-region replication copy was stuck at 20 Mbps on a 1 Gbps link; the window was too small for the BDP.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "We are building a multiplayer game for mobile. Players send position updates 30 times per second to a game server. Use TCP so nothing gets lost, right?" About 50k concurrent players, 60-byte updates, typical mobile loss 1-2%, RTT 80 ms.
questions.promptHtml: What transport do you propose, and what do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "TCP because it is reliable" or "UDP because it is fast". Neither says what is lost and why that matters.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which messages must be reliable (purchases, chat) versus disposable (positions)? Is there a latency budget (say under 100 ms for input)? Do we need to support networks that block UDP? Who owns the client update path, so we can ship a custom protocol?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I split traffic into two classes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Positions are stale after 33 ms, so a retransmit is worthless. With TCP, if packet 17 is lost, packets 18 to 20 wait about 1 RTT (80 ms) behind it: head-of-line blocking makes the game stutter. Other facts: purchases and chat need ordering and delivery.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype both and compare p99 update-to-render delay under emulated 2% loss (tc netem).
  5. Root cause: TCP's in-order guarantee is the wrong semantic for state that is superseded by the next packet.
  6. Fix: UDP (or QUIC datagrams/WebRTC) for positions, keep each datagram under about 1,200 bytes to avoid fragmentation, add sequence numbers so the client drops old ones; a TCP or reliable-stream channel for purchases and chat. Prefer an existing library over inventing reliability.
  7. Prevention: Rate-limit per client (UDP has no congestion control, so we must control rate ourselves), amplification checks, TCP fallback for networks that block UDP.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hand-roll full reliability over UDP; I own reliability and fairness then, an expensive choice that is only reversible if clients can be updated.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Corporate Wi-Fi blocks UDP? -> Fall back to a TCP/WebSocket path with degraded expectations.
  • Spectator mode needs every event? -> Reliable stream for that class.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped TCP-only for positions and saw jittery movement only for users on lossy mobile links; desktop QA never reproduced it because the lab network had zero loss.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one protocol for everything.
  • Hire: UDP for positions with the HOL reasoning, TCP for critical messages.
  • Strong hire: also covers datagram size, rate control, fallback and use of an existing protocol.

questions.contextHtml:
Order API behind an AWS ALB, clients are mobile backends using a pooled HTTP/1.1 client. About 1,500 req/s at peak, but quiet periods at night. Error rate alert fires every morning at 06:00 right after quiet hours: 0.3% of requests fail, then it fades.

06:00:02 ERROR java.net.SocketException: Connection reset
06:00:02 ELB 502 count=41 (target 200 OK, backend CPU 12%)
nginx keepalive_timeout 75s; ALB idle timeout 60s; client pool idle eviction 120s

A teammate blames the new deploy from yesterday.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds blind retries everywhere and raises backend capacity; CPU is 12% so capacity is the red herring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do errors follow idle gaps, not load? Are the failing calls on reused connections? Which hop sends the RST (ALB logs vs app logs)? Were there deploys before earlier mornings with the same pattern?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Retry idempotent requests once on connection reset; for non-idempotent ones use idempotency keys.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The pool holds connections idle up to 120 s but ALB closes at 60 s, so the client reuses a dead connection; (b) deploy bug (does not explain the time pattern); (c) backend overload (CPU 12%, no).
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate error timestamps with time-since-last-use of the connection; tcpdump a failing connection to see the FIN/RST from the LB side; check ALB access logs for 502s with no target response.
  5. Root cause: Idle timeouts disagree: client 120 s > ALB 60 s. Quiet night hours leave pooled connections idle for over 60 s; the first requests in the morning use closed sockets.
  6. Fix: Short-term: client idle eviction 45 s (client < LB < server, e.g. server 75 s). Long-term: enable background validation or TCP keepalive 30 s, retry on idempotent calls.
  7. Prevention: Keep the timeout chain in one documented config; alert on 502 count with low backend latency; a test that idles a connection past the LB timeout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising the ALB timeout to hide it (costs LB resources and still mismatches), and not retrying non-idempotent POSTs blindly (double orders).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does a deploy make it worse? -> Fresh pool replaces idle, so deploys can mask it; it returns after quiet periods.
  • Does HTTP/2 fix it? -> No, same idle-close race; use PING/keepalive.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payment client saw random resets only on Mondays; weekend traffic idled the pool beyond the LB timeout. Lowering eviction to 45 s removed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales up servers.
  • Hire: spots idle timeout mismatch and fixes ordering.
  • Strong hire: verifies with packet capture, adds idempotent retries and alerting.

questions.contextHtml: A download service in Mumbai serves 2 MB JSON bundles to apps in Virginia. Customers have 1 Gbps links, RTT 200 ms, yet each fetch takes about 2.5 s. Server CPU and network are idle. The infra team proposes upgrading everyone to a 10 Gbps link. Each fetch opens a fresh connection.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to buy more bandwidth; ignores RTT.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a connection reused between fetches? What TLS version? Can the payload be compressed or split? Is a CDN allowed near Virginia?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable gzip/brotli on JSON; reuse connections.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Slow start round trips dominate; handshake RTTs; small receiver window; packet loss.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -ti for cwnd growth; curl timing (time_connect, time_starttransfer, time_total); capture and look at the flights per RTT.
  5. Root cause: Math: handshake 200 ms, TLS 1.3 200 ms, then initial cwnd 10 segments (14 KB) doubling: 14, 28, 56, 112, 224, 448, 896 KB, about 8 RTT = 1.6 s before 2 MB is delivered, total about 2.0 to 2.5 s. Link speed is irrelevant: the limit is round trips.
  6. Fix: Long-lived pooled/HTTP/2 connection (window already grown, set tcp_slow_start_after_idle=0), compress to about 400 KB (3 fewer RTT), CDN or regional edge to cut RTT, HTTP/3 for 1-RTT setup.
  7. Prevention: Budget latency in RTTs in design reviews; synthetic tests from the far region.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising initial cwnd on kernels blindly (hurts fairness); CDN adds cost but is reversible.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the payload were 10 GB? -> Then BDP and window scaling matter; bandwidth becomes the limit.
  • Does BBR help? -> Only if loss is the limiter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent a quarter on bigger pipes; moving the same bundle to a regional edge with a warm connection cut p50 from 2.5 s to 0.6 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more bandwidth.
  • Hire: explains slow start and reuse.
  • Strong hire: numeric RTT budget, compression and edge, and states when bandwidth would matter.

questions.promptHtml: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests, yet people say it still has head-of-line blocking. Explain, and say how HTTP/3 changes that.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests layered thinking: HOL at the HTTP layer versus the transport layer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HTTP/1.1 had HOL at the HTTP layer (one request at a time per connection). HTTP/2 fixed that by interleaving streams, but all streams share one TCP connection, which delivers bytes strictly in order. One lost packet stalls every stream until it is resent. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, where each stream has its own ordering, so loss stalls only the stream that owned the packet.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP/2: Stream A, B, C -> ONE TCP byte stream -> a lost packet blocks all three
HTTP/3: Stream A, B, C -> QUIC streams (over UDP) -> loss on A blocks only A

At 2% loss and 80 ms RTT, each loss costs at least 1 RTT (fast retransmit), more on a timeout (200 ms or more). With h2 that delay hits all parallel streams; with h3 only one. Gains are largest on poor mobile links and small on clean wired links. Also, 6 parallel h1.1 connections are independent, so under heavy loss h1.1 can sometimes feel better than a single h2 connection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying HTTP/2 removed HOL blocking completely.
  • Saying HTTP/3 is always faster.
  • Forgetting that QPACK exists to avoid header compression creating new cross-stream blocking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a phone switching Wi-Fi to 4G break h2? -> Yes, the 4-tuple changes; QUIC uses a connection ID and survives.
  2. Why did QUIC not extend TCP? -> TCP lives in kernels and middleboxes; too hard to change.
  3. What is the cost? -> More CPU (user-space packets, per-packet encryption) and UDP-block fallback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE says h3 is faster. Senior says where (lossy mobile), where not (clean wired), and the CPU cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After enabling h3 at the edge a team saw p99 improve only for mobile users, and origin CPU rise slightly.

questions.contextHtml:
Service A calls Service B over gRPC. B has 8 pods behind an L4 (TCP) load balancer. A has 4 pods, each opens a few long-lived connections. Traffic is 6,000 RPC/s.

pod   cpu   rps
b-1   92%   3900
b-2   85%   2100
b-3-8  2%     0

Autoscaler keeps adding pods but the new ones stay idle. Latency p99 is 1.8 s.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the load lopsided and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the balancing algorithm (round robin) or the new pods' readiness.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How many connections does each A pod open? L4 or L7 LB? Do connections live for hours? Is there a max connection age?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart A pods one at a time (reconnect spreads), or raise the connection count; does not last.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: L4 balances connections, not requests, and h2 multiplexes everything on a few connections; sticky long-lived connections; autoscaled pods get no new connections because nobody reconnects; uneven per-request cost (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -tn dst :50051 on A pods (2 to 3 connections each); LB connection counts per backend; per-pod RPS metrics.
  5. Root cause: HTTP/2 puts hundreds of streams in one TCP connection, the L4 balancer picked a backend once at connect time, so 4 pods x 2 connections = 8 connections spread by luck, not by load.
  6. Fix: Short term: set max connection age (e.g. 5 min with a grace period) so clients reconnect and rebalance. Long term: L7 proxy (Envoy) balancing per request, or client-side balancing with service discovery.
  7. Prevention: Test load distribution with scale-out events; alert on per-pod RPS skew.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not more pods (they stay idle). Max connection age causes reconnect storms if synchronized: add jitter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would HTTP/1.1 behave the same? -> Less, because each request would use a pool of many connections.
  • Cost of L7 proxy? -> Extra hop and CPU, in exchange for per-request balancing and retries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team doubled B's pods twice before noticing none of the new pods took traffic; a max-connection-age setting rebalanced in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks algorithm.
  • Hire: connection vs request balancing, L7 or client-side.
  • Strong hire: connection age with jitter and verifies with per-pod metrics.

questions.contextHtml:
A report-rendering service calls an internal PDF API at 1 fixed IP:port, about 800 req/s, using a new HTTP/1.1 connection per call with Connection: close. At peak:

java.net.BindException: Cannot assign requested address
$ ss -s   ->  TCP: 31204 (estab 210, closed 30650, timewait 30610)
$ sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range -> 32768 60999

CPU and memory are fine; the PDF API is healthy.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restart the service or tell the API team to add servers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who closes the connection? Is the destination one IP:port? Is a proxy/NAT in the path? Can the client use keep-alive?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Widen the port range or add a second destination IP/port temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: TIME_WAIT sockets exhaust the ephemeral range; port leak in app; NAT limits.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l; check the leak with ESTAB count (210, no leak).
  5. Root cause: 800 conn/s x 60 s TIME_WAIT = about 48k sockets wanted, but only about 28k ports exist for the single destination 4-tuple. The client closes first so it holds TIME_WAIT.
  6. Fix: Keep-alive pooling (kills the problem; also saves a handshake RTT per call). Optional: more destination IPs.
  7. Prevention: Alert on timewait count and ephemeral port use; lint against clients without pooling.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not shortening TIME_WAIT or enabling risky recycling hacks (breaks behind NAT, may corrupt connections); not scaling the healthy API.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Server closes first instead? -> The server holds TIME_WAIT, shifting the problem.
  • Would h2 help? -> One connection, yes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly batch failed every 40 minutes with bind errors; a shared HTTP client singleton with a pool ended it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart.
  • Hire: names TIME_WAIT and pooling.
  • Strong hire: does the 800 x 60 vs 28k math and rejects unsafe sysctl hacks.

questions.contextHtml:
You front a mobile app (6M DAU, peak 12k req/s) with a CDN. Product wants HTTP/3 to cut tail latency. After enabling it for 10% of traffic:

metric                   h2        h3
p50 latency (ms)         180       170
p99 latency mobile (ms)  2400      1500
p99 latency wifi (ms)    420       430
edge CPU per req         1.0x      1.6x
h3 share of requests     -         4.1%   (expected about 10%)

A VP says the rollout "does not work" because only 4.1% used h3.
questions.promptHtml: Interpret these numbers and decide the rollout plan.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rolls back due to CPU, or declares victory on the average.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How do clients discover h3? Do clients fall back? Which networks block UDP 443? Is origin connection also h3? What is the CPU budget?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; fallback keeps users working.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Discovery: clients start on h2, learn via Alt-Svc or the HTTPS DNS record, upgrade next visit, so share lags the rollout; UDP blocked on some networks causes fallback; the gains are largest on lossy mobile (p99 2400 to 1500) and nil on Wi-Fi (as expected).
  4. How I'd verify each: Edge logs by protocol and network type; count Alt-Svc responses and client fallbacks; check UDP 443 reachability from RUM data.
  5. Root cause: Nothing is broken. 4.1% is a discovery lag plus blocked UDP; the CPU cost is user-space QUIC and per-packet encryption.
  6. Fix: Keep going: raise to 50% then 100% at the edge, keep h2 and h1.1 as fallback, watch h3 share trending toward the achievable ceiling. Keep origin on h1/h2.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards split by protocol and network; capacity plan for 1.6x edge CPU on h3 traffic; do not make business logic depend on h3.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Edge-only is reversible and cheap; end-to-end QUIC internally costs CPU with immature tooling, so skip it. I would not report only global averages, which hide the mobile win.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Security team asks about 0-RTT? -> Allow only for idempotent GETs, replay risk.
  • Load balancer needs changes? -> Route by connection ID, not 4-tuple, if you run your own.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rollout looked flat on mean latency; slicing by network type showed a 35% p99 win on cellular that justified the CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: judges by the global average.
  • Hire: explains discovery lag and the mobile-only gain.
  • Strong hire: staged plan, fallback, CPU budget, protocol-sliced metrics.

questions.promptHtml: What does QUIC give you over TCP+TLS, and what are the risks of 0-RTT? Would you run QUIC inside your data centre?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who repeat "QUIC is faster" from those who know the mechanism, security trade-off and cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: QUIC runs on UDP in user space and merges transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes: 1 RTT for a new connection (versus 2 for TCP+TLS1.3) and 0-RTT on resumption. Streams are independent, and a connection ID lets the connection survive IP changes. The risk of 0-RTT is replay, so only idempotent requests. Inside a data centre I would usually not: RTT is tiny, CPU cost is higher, tooling less mature; I keep it at the edge.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RTT 100 ms: h2 over TCP+TLS1.3 new connection = 200 ms before the request; h3 = 100 ms; resumed 0-RTT = 0 ms. 0-RTT data is sent in the first flight under a key from an earlier session, and an attacker can replay that packet, so a non-idempotent POST could execute twice. Mitigations: allow 0-RTT only for GET-like requests, or have servers enforce anti-replay. Because QUIC encrypts headers and has its own reliability and congestion control, it is not unreliable UDP. Costs: about 2x CPU in early reports (verify for your stack), some networks block UDP 443 so clients need TCP fallback, and L4 balancers must route by connection ID.

Client -> QUIC 1-RTT handshake -> Server
Client -> 0-RTT data on resume -> Server   (replayable)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "QUIC is UDP so unreliable".
  • Allowing 0-RTT on payment endpoints.
  • No TCP fallback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does migration work? -> Connection ID identifies the connection, not IP:port; the path is validated after a change.
  2. Why user space? -> Faster evolution than kernel TCP, but costs CPU.
  3. How do you protect 0-RTT endpoints? -> Idempotency keys plus server anti-replay and limiting 0-RTT to safe methods.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists features. Senior states the replay threat, the CPU price, the fallback requirement and the edge-only decision.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled 0-RTT broadly and saw duplicate order attempts; limiting it to GET fixed it.

questions.contextHtml:
A rolling deploy of the API tier (200 pods, 50k persistent client connections, mostly mobile apps) restarted all pods in 3 minutes. At 14:02:

14:02 new TLS handshakes/s: 400 -> 38,000
14:02 api cpu: 35% -> 98% (kernel + crypto)
14:03 connect timeouts (1s) -> clients retry immediately -> 61,000 handshakes/s
14:07 error rate 41%, recovers 14:19 after manual scale to 3x

Postmortem is on Monday.
questions.promptHtml: Give the review: causes, contributing factors and actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Human error in the deploy" and "add more servers".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did pods drain connections gracefully? Do clients use backoff and jitter? Is TLS terminated on the API pods or at an LB? Is session resumption working?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the rollout, scale out (done at 14:19), shed load at the edge with a rate limit on new connections.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Synchronized reconnect after killing pods; a retry storm from the 1 s connect timeout with no backoff; handshake CPU cost (TCP + TLS per connection); low session resumption hit rate; capacity headroom only for steady state.
  4. How I'd verify each: Handshake rate graph vs deploy events; client retry logs timing; TLS resumption ratio; CPU profile (crypto vs kernel).
  5. Root cause: Deploy dropped connections all at once, clients reconnected simultaneously, and immediate retries amplified 400/s to 61k/s of handshakes (a metastable retry storm).
  6. Fix: Connection draining (stop accepting, send GOAWAY or close in waves), maxSurge and slower rollout, client exponential backoff with jitter, session resumption, handshake offload at the edge.
  7. Prevention: Load test a full-fleet reconnect, alert on handshake rate, canary first, cap retries (retry budget).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just 3x permanent capacity (costly and the next storm exceeds it); no longer connect timeouts alone, which only delays failure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Move TLS to an L7 LB? -> Shifts the CPU, still needs draining.
  • Would QUIC reduce it? -> Cheaper handshake RTTs, not CPU, and migration helps clients keep connections.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fleet of 100k IoT clients reconnected in lockstep every deploy until a randomized 0 to 30 s delay was added to the client.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames a person.
  • Hire: draining, jittered backoff, slower rollout.
  • Strong hire: quantifies amplification, retry budgets and a full-reconnect load test.

questions.contextHtml: A legacy web shop serves about 60 assets per page over HTTP/1.1 using domain sharding (img1..img4.shop.com), sprite sheets and a single 2 MB JS bundle. Users are 70% mobile, RTT 50 ms, loss 1%. The CDN supports h2 and h3. An architect says: "Enable h2 and delete the sharding; it will fix everything." Another says: "Leave it; it works."
questions.promptHtml: Decide: what do you change, in what order, and what could go wrong?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Flips the switch and keeps all old workarounds, or removes them all at once without measuring.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the current LCP and p95 page load by device? Is the origin h1 behind the CDN? Do we have RUM to compare? Any third-party assets on other hosts?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable h2 at the CDN, which is reversible and needs no code change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: h2 multiplexing gets the 60 resources in about 1 RTT instead of about 10 rounds (about 500 ms of waiting at 50 ms); sharding now hurts (extra handshakes, lost HPACK and shared congestion window); on 1% loss TCP HOL stalls all streams, so h3 adds value on mobile.
  4. How I'd verify each: A/B with RUM per protocol; WebPageTest on throttled 4G; compare waterfalls.
  5. Root cause: The old rules (bundle, shard) were workarounds for 6 connections per host, not goals.
  6. Fix: Order: (1) enable h2 at CDN; (2) collapse shards to one host in steps, measuring; (3) split the 2 MB bundle so caching works per module (bundling is less needed); (4) enable h3 for mobile with fallback; keep sprites only where measured useful.
  7. Prevention: Performance budget in CI, protocol-sliced RUM dashboard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on server push (deprecated, Chrome removed it); not make h2 the cause for one big TCP window; changes are reversible, so ship incrementally rather than in one big bang.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Origin speaks only h1.1? -> Fine; terminate h2/h3 at the CDN, origin pool with keep-alive.
  • Is pipelining the same as multiplexing? -> No; pipelining kept strict order and was disabled in browsers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team removed sharding the same day h2 was enabled, saw a regression from a cold cache after hash changes, and learned to stage it with measurement.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-or-nothing change.
  • Hire: enable h2, remove sharding, bundle rethink, measure.
  • Strong hire: staged plan with RUM, h3 for lossy mobile, and clear reversibility reasoning.
